{{nihongo|'''Masakazu "Mark" Konishi'''|小西 正一|Konishi Masakazu|February 17, 1933 – July 23, 2020}} was a Japanese [[Neuroscientist|neurobiologist]], known for his research on the neuroscience underlying the behavior of [[owls]] and [[songbirds]].<ref name=Caltech/><ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Masakazu (Mark) Konishi|url=https://www.bbe.caltech.edu/people/masakazu-mark-konishi|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200109004059/http://www.bbe.caltech.edu/people/masakazu-mark-konishi|archive-date=January 9, 2020|access-date=July 25, 2020|website=Caltech: The Division of Biology and Biological Engineering}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Konishi was born on February 17, 1933, in Kyoto, Japan, the only child of poor [[Nishijin-ori|"Nishijin" weavers]].<ref name="Caltech" /><ref name=":3">{{Cite book|last=Konishi|first=Masakazu|url=https://www.oxfordscholarship.com/view/10.1093/acprof:oso/9780195380101.001.0001/acprof-9780195380101-chapter-7|title=The History of Neuroscience in Autobiography|publisher=[[Society for Neuroscience]]|year=2009|isbn=9780195380101|editor-last=Squire|editor-first=Larry R.|pages=227–264|chapter=Masakazu Konishi|doi=10.1093/acprof:oso/9780195380101.003.0007}}</ref> As a child during the [[World War II|Second World War]], he grew edible plants in his family's backyard and rooftop, and raised [[Rabbit|rabbits]] for food.<ref name=":3" /> In his spare time, he enjoyed playing with animals, including insects, fish, birds, rabbits, and dogs.<ref name=":3" />

He first studied at [[Hokkaido University]], where he completed his [[Bachelor of Science]] in 1956 and [[Master of Science]] in 1958.<ref name="Caltech" /><ref name=":0" /> He had initially planned to study [[agriculture]], but changed his mind upon seeing the [[zoology]] subjects on offer.<ref name=":3" /> Despite finding most of these zoology lectures "quite boring", his interest was piqued by the [[neurophysiology]] course taught by Mitsuo Tamashige.<ref name=":3" /> His master's research examined [[Brood parasite|brood parasitism]] of [[Acrocephalus (bird)|reed warbler]] nests by [[Cuckoo|cuckoos]].<ref name=":3" />

Konishi received a [[Fulbright Program|Fulbright travel scholarship]] to move to the [[United States]] for his doctoral research.<ref name=":3" /> In September 1958, he arrived at the [[University of California, Berkeley]] to undertake his PhD with [[Alden H. Miller]], only to discover that Miller was on sabbatical in [[South America]].<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last1=Ball |first1=Gregory F. |last2=Dooling |first2=Robert J. |author-link2=Robert Dooling |date=September 27, 2017 |title=Peter R. Marler, 1928–2014 |journal=The Auk |volume=134 |issue=4 |pages=932–934 |doi=10.1642/AUK-17-135.1 |s2cid=89957289 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Instead, he completed his PhD under ethologist [[Peter Marler]], who had also recently arrived at the institution.<ref name=":2" /> Konishi's findings highlighted the important role of auditory feedback in [[songbird]] [[vocal learning]], using [[White-crowned sparrow|white-crowned sparrows]] and other songbird species.<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Konishi|first=Masakazu|date=1965|title=The Role of Auditory Feedback in the Control of Vocalization in the White-Crowned Sparrow|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1439-0310.1965.tb01688.x|journal=Zeitschrift für Tierpsychologie|volume=22|issue=7|pages=770–783|doi=10.1111/j.1439-0310.1965.tb01688.x|pmid=5874921|url-access=subscription}}</ref> His work, together with that of fellow PhD student [[Fernando Nottebohm]], "laid the foundation for the discovery of the avian song control system by Nottebohm in the 1970s and the remarkable development of the field of birdsong neurobiology."<ref name=":2" />

== Career ==
[[File:'Tutoke' - geograph.org.uk - 2532332.jpg|thumb|Konishi was noted for his research on hearing in [[Barn-owl|barn owls]].]]
Following his graduation in 1963,<ref name=":0" /> Konishi undertook two postdoctoral positions in [[Germany]], at the [[University of Tübingen]] (1963–64) and in the Division of Experimental Neurophysiology at the [[Max Planck Society|Max-Planck Institute]] (1964–65).<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":1">{{Cite web|last=Konishi|first=Masakazu|date=February 6, 2017|title=How the Owl Tracks Its Prey|url=https://www.americanscientist.org/article/how-the-owl-tracks-its-prey|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200725055219/https://www.americanscientist.org/article/how-the-owl-tracks-its-prey|archive-date=July 25, 2020|access-date=July 25, 2020|website=American Scientist|language=en}}</ref> He then returned to the United States, working at the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison|University of Wisconsin]] (1965–66) and later at [[Princeton University]] (1966–75).<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":1" /> During this time, Konishi began research projects exploring [[owl]] and songbird behavior.<ref name=":3" />

While based at Princeton, Konishi attempted to use neurophysiological methods to measure hearing in birds, by determining the threshold sensitivities of single [[Neuron|neurons]] in the [[Cochlear nucleus|cochlear nuclei]]: all species tested could hear low frequencies, but species with high frequencies in their songs could also hear high frequencies.<ref name=":3" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Konishi|first=Masakazu|date=1970|title=Comparative Neurophysiological Studies of Hearing and Vocalizations in Songbirds|url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF00297829|journal=Zeitschrift für vergleichende Physiologie|volume=66|issue=3|pages=257–72|doi=10.1007/BF00297829|s2cid=40427812|url-access=subscription}}</ref> He also investigated the development of hearing in duck embryos.<ref name=":3" /> Konishi's research on owls began when he acquired three nestling [[Barn-owl|barn owls]] from a local [[Birdwatching|birdwatcher]].<ref name=":3" />

Konishi was a Professor of Biology at [[California Institute of Technology]] (Caltech) from 1975 to 1980, and served as Bing Professor from 1980 until his retirement in 2013.<ref name="Caltech" /><ref name=":0" /> In the 1980s, he and his collaborators raised white-crowned sparrows in isolation, and demonstrated that these birds still preferred their own species' song over heterospecific songs from the same geographic area.<ref name=":3" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Konishi|first=Masakazu|date=1985|title=Birdsong: From behavior to neuron|journal=Annual Review of Neuroscience|volume=8|issue=1|pages=125–170|doi=10.1146/annurev.ne.08.030185.001013|pmid=3885827}}</ref>

Konishi was a leader in the field of avian neuroethology and a foremost expert in avian auditory systems.<ref name="Caltech" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Masakazu Konishi {{!}} Gruber Foundation |url=https://gruber.yale.edu/neuroscience/masakazu-konishi |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221009111316/https://gruber.yale.edu/neuroscience/masakazu-konishi |archive-date=October 9, 2022|access-date=July 27, 2020 |website=gruber.yale.edu}}</ref> Throughout his career, he advised dozens of graduate students and postdoctoral researchers.<ref name="Caltech" /> Among his Caltech students was [[Larry Katz]], whom Konishi described as his "most adventurous and skillful" student.<ref name=":3" /><ref name="Katz">{{Cite journal|last1=Bargmann|first1=Cori|last2=Mason|first2=Carol|date=December 22, 2005|title=In Appreciation of Lawrence C. Katz, 1956–2005|journal=Neuron|volume=48|issue=6|pages=897–900|doi=10.1016/j.neuron.2005.12.012|pmid=16450476|s2cid=16423367|doi-access=free}}</ref> Katz introduced brain slice techniques into Konishi's lab.<ref name=":3" /> Work by students in the lab, including Katz, Mark Gurney and Jim McCasland, helped establish that neurons in the songbirds' [[HVC (avian brain region)|HVC]] respond to sound and are selective for the bird's own song.<ref name=":3" />

Konishi was a member of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] (1979)<ref name=":3" /> and the [[National Academy of Sciences]] (1985).<ref name=":3" /> He was a founding member of the International Society for Neuroethology,<ref name=":3" /> and served as the society's second President from 1986 to 1989.<ref name="Caltech" /><ref name=":3" />

== Personal life and death ==
In his spare time, Konishi enjoyed working with animals, writing "I have been lucky, because I did not have to go far from my hobby to my scientific subjects."<ref name=":3" /> In his later years, he began training [[Border Collie|border collies]] to herd [[sheep]].<ref name=":3" />

In 1990, Konishi received the [[International Prize for Biology]], which was established to honor [[Hirohito]], the Shōwa Emperor of Japan (1901–1989).<ref name="Caltech" /><ref name=":3" /> When receiving the award, he met [[Akihito]], son of [[Hirohito]], and his wife [[Empress Michiko]].<ref name=":3" /> Several years later, the imperial couple invited Konishi to dine at their palace.<ref name=":3" /> The couple did not say a word about the Japanese food he had chosen during the meal; nevertheless, Konishi found the Empress particularly "charming" and, later, sent her a reel of tape containing the song of [[Common nightingale|European nightingales]].<ref name=":3" /> She thanked him in a handwritten letter.<ref name=":3" />

Konishi retired from his position at Caltech in 2013, and died of [[old age|natural causes]] at his home in [[San Diego]], [[California]] on July 23, 2020, at the age of 87.<ref name="Caltech">{{Cite web|title=Mark Konishi, Renowned Neuroethologist, Dies at 87|url=https://www.caltech.edu/about/news/mark-konishi-renowned-neuroethologist-dies-87|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200725053121/https://www.caltech.edu/about/news/mark-konishi-renowned-neuroethologist-dies-87|archive-date=July 25, 2020|access-date=July 25, 2020|website=[[California Institute of Technology]]|language=en}}</ref>
